hero.title: The Company Rule (1773-1858)
hero.description: Master the constitutional and administrative milestones of the East India Company Rule, from the Regulating Act of 1773 to the Charter Act of 1853 (UPSC GS Paper-2: Historical Underpinnings).

mockIntro.title: Interactive UPSC Mock Test
mockIntro.description: Assess your understanding of administrative acts, centralization features, and Charter reforms. This timed test contains 10 high-yield, exam-standard questions with negative marking.

timeline.title: Chronological Milestones of Company Rule
timeline.description: Key legislative changes marking the evolution of British administration in India.

cards.details: First step by the British Parliament to regulate EIC affairs. Established Governor-General of Bengal (Warren Hastings) and Supreme Court at Calcutta (1774).
Distinguished EIC's commercial and political functions, creating the Board of Control and starting the system of Double Government.
Ended EIC's trade monopoly in India (except in tea and China trade). Allowed Christian missionaries and allotted Rs 1 Lakh for education.
Final step toward centralization. Created Governor-General of India (William Bentinck), stripped Bombay/Madras of legislative powers, and ended EIC's commercial functions.
Separated legislative and executive functions of GG's Council, created the Central Legislative Council, and introduced open competition for civil services.

mnemonics.title: Mnemonics & Memory Hacks
mnemonics.description: Visual hooks to memorize complex details of the Charter Acts for UPSC.

items.title: Mnemonic 1: Charter Act of 1813
items.decryption: Remember 1813 provisions: **T**ea & China trade monopoly retained; **E**ducation funding (Rs 1 Lakh) initiated (**Teacher**); Christian **Missionaries** allowed entry; Trade **Monopoly** ended otherwise.

items.title: Mnemonic 2: Charter Act of 1833
items.decryption: Remember 1833 provisions: Lord William **Bentinck** becomes first GGI; EIC becomes a purely **Administrative** body (no trade); **B**ombay & Madras deprived of legislative powers; **L**aw Member Macaulay added to Council.

items.title: Mnemonic 3: Charter Act of 1853
items.decryption: Remember 1853 provisions: **Separate** executive and legislative Council duties; **Open** competition introduced for Civil Services; **Central** Legislative Council (mini-**Parliament**) established with local representation.

flashcards.title: Active Recall Flashcards
flashcards.description: Quick active recall drill to test legislative facts before attempting practice questions.

items.question: Who was the first Governor-General of Bengal, and which act created the post?
items.answer: Warren Hastings. The post was created by the Regulating Act of 1773, which renamed the Governor of Bengal.

items.question: Which act established the system of 'Double Government' consisting of Board of Control and Court of Directors?
items.answer: Pitt's India Act of 1784. It separated EIC's commercial affairs (Directors) and political affairs (Board of Control).

items.question: Which charter act ended the trade monopoly of EIC in India completely?
items.answer: The Charter Act of 1833. (The Charter Act of 1813 only ended the monopoly *except* in tea and China trade).

items.question: By which act was Lord Macaulay appointed as the first Law Member of the Governor-General's Council?
items.answer: The Charter Act of 1833, which added a fourth member (Law Member) to the GG's Executive Council.

items.question: Which act introduced local representation in the Indian (Central) Legislative Council for the first time?
items.answer: The Charter Act of 1853, which allowed local governments of Madras, Bombay, Bengal, and Agra to nominate 4 of the 6 new legislative councilors.

traps.title: UPSC Civil Services Exam Traps to Avoid
items: Trap 1: Confusing the Governor-General of **Bengal** (Warren Hastings, 1773) with the Governor-General of **India** (William Bentinck, 1833).
Trap 2: Assuming EIC trade monopoly in India ended completely in 1813. Sourcing shows EIC retained its monopoly in **tea trade** and **China trade** until the Charter Act of 1833.
Trap 3: Confusing the *attempt* to introduce open competition for civil services (Charter Act 1833, which failed due to Court of Directors opposition) with its *actual* enactment (Charter Act 1853).

Trap 4: Thinking EIC rule was terminated by the Charter Act of 1853. The EIC rule was actually terminated by the **Government of India Act 1858** following the Revolt of 1857; the 1853 Act only left the time limit unspecified, signaling that Crown takeover was imminent.

deepDive.title: Syllabus Core Study Notes (Deep-Dive)
deepDive.description: Explore the evolution of British legislative supremacy and administrative centralization.

sections.title: 1. Foundation of Centralisation: Regulating Act 1773 & Pitt's India Act 1784
sections.content:
The Regulating Act of 1773 initiated parliamentary control over the East India Company, which was further refined by the system of double government under Pitt's India Act of 1784.

Regulating Act of 1773 & Amending Act 1781
  • Governor-General of Bengal: Warren Hastings became the first GG of Bengal. A 4-member Executive Council was added, with decisions based on majority and GG holding a casting vote.
  • Supreme Court Calcutta: Established in 1774 (1 Chief Justice + 3 Judges). Elijah Impey was first CJ.
  • Exemptions (1781 Act): The Amending Act of 1781 (Act of Settlement) resolved executive-judicial conflicts by exempting the GG, Council, and EIC servants from SC jurisdiction for official acts, and excluding revenue administration.
Pitt's India Act 1784 & Double Government
  • Functional Separation: Commercial affairs remained under the Court of Directors. Political, civil, and military affairs went to the newly created Board of Control (6 Crown commissioners).
  • Crown Supremacy: EIC's territories were designated as 'British possessions in India' for the first time.
  • Executive Reduction: Reduced GG council strength from 4 to 3 members to ease majority voting.

sections.title: 2. Progression of Monopoly and Crown Sovereignty: Charter Acts of 1793 & 1813
sections.content:
The Charter Acts of 1793 and 1813 systematically asserted Crown sovereignty and dismantled the trade monopoly of the East India Company in response to domestic commercial lobbies.

Feature Charter Act 1793 Charter Act 1813 Charter Act 1833 Charter Act 1853
Trade Monopoly Extended EIC monopoly for 20 years. Ended monopoly, except for tea and China trade. Completely ended commercial monopoly and EIC trade. No fixed period extension; company retained trust.
Head of Govt Governor-General of Bengal (overriding powers confirmed). Governor-General of Bengal (Crown sovereignty asserted). Governor-General of India (Lord William Bentinck). Governor-General of India (Legislative separated from Executive).
Legislative Rights Overriding powers extended to all future GGs. Sovereignty of the British Crown declared. Bombay/Madras lost legislative rights; GGI got central laws. New Legislative Council established (6 new members).
Civil Services Reserved senior posts for covenanted servants. No major changes. Attempted to introduce open competition (vetoed by Directors). Successfully introduced open competition (Macaulay Committee).
Act of 1786 and Charter Act of 1793
  • Act of 1786: Granted Cornwallis overriding powers over his Executive Council in special cases and appointed him Commander-in-Chief.
  • Monopoly Extension: The 1793 Act extended EIC's trade monopoly for 20 years and extended overriding powers to all future GGs.
  • Indian Revenue payments: Board of Control members and staff salaries were charged to EIC Indian revenues, a practice that continued until 1919.
Charter Act of 1813: Breaking the Monopoly
  • Monopoly Abolished: Trade monopoly in India was abolished due to pressure from British manufacturers, except for **tea trade** and **China trade**.
  • Crown Sovereignty: Formally declared the sovereignty of the British Crown over Indian territories.
  • Missionaries & Education: Allowed Christian missionaries to enter India. Provided a statutory grant of **Rs 1 Lakh annually** to promote education and science.

sections.title: 3. Peak Centralisation and Separation of Powers: Charter Acts of 1833 & 1853
sections.content:
The final phase of Company Rule saw peak administrative centralization under the Charter Act of 1833 and the initial separation of legislative functions under the Charter Act of 1853.

Charter Act of 1833: Peak Centralisation
  • Governor-General of India: Lord William Bentinck became the first GGI. Vested with full civil, military, and exclusive legislative powers. Bombay and Madras lost legislative authority.
  • Purely Administrative: Commercial operations of EIC ended completely, including tea/China trade.
  • Law Member & Codification: A Law Member (Macaulay) was added to the Council. First Law Commission appointed in 1834 to codify all Indian laws (resulting in the IPC).
  • Attempted Open Competition: Attempted open competition for civil services, but EIC directors opposed.
Charter Act of 1853: Separation of Powers
  • Indian Legislative Council: Added 6 new 'legislative councilors' to the Council. Separated legislative and executive functions for the first time, creating a mini-parliament.
  • Civil Services Open Competition: Enacted open competition for civil service recruitments. Macaulay Committee on Civil Services appointed in 1854.
  • Local Representation: 4 of 6 legislative councilors appointed by local governments of Madras, Bombay, Bengal, and Agra.
  • Unspecified Charter Term: EIC rule extended without a fixed timeline, signaling Crown takeover.
